title: What Claude is, and isn't
why: Knowing how Claude produces an answer tells you when to lean on it and when to double-check.
idea: Claude is a large language model. It writes by predicting what text should come next, one small piece at a time, based on everything in the conversation so far. Trained at huge scale, that simple process makes it very good at drafting, explaining, summarizing, and working through problems.

The same process explains its limits. It can say something false in a confident voice, a failure called hallucination. Without web search, it doesn't know about events after its training cutoff. And it only knows what you've told it about your situation.
So treat Claude like a fast, well-read collaborator who has never met you: give it context, and check the parts that matter.

try.intro: Test Claude on a subject you already know well, so you can judge the answer yourself.
try.prompt: Explain [a topic you know well, like your job, a hobby, or your hometown] to a curious 12-year-old in under 150 words. Then list two things people commonly get wrong about it.
steps: Open Claude and start a new chat.
Paste the prompt and replace the bracketed part.
Read the answer as the expert you are.

check: I found at least one thing it got right that I'd want a beginner to know.
I looked for anything oversimplified or wrong, and noted it.
I can explain in one sentence why Claude can sound sure and still be wrong.

quiz.q: How does Claude produce an answer?
options: It looks up a stored answer in a database
It predicts likely text, piece by piece, from the conversation so far
It copies the most popular web page on the topic
A person reviews and writes each reply
quiz.explain: Language models generate text by predicting what comes next. That's why answers are fluent, and also why they can be fluently wrong.

quiz.q: You ask about something that happened yesterday, and web search is off. What should you expect?
options: Claude may not know, or may guess
Claude will refuse to talk about news
quiz.explain: Without search, Claude only knows what was in its training data, which stops at its knowledge cutoff.

title: Say what good looks like
why: Most disappointing answers come from prompts that leave Claude guessing about the goal, the reader, or the finish line.
idea: A strong prompt answers four questions: What do you want? Who is it for? What does Claude need to know? What does a good result look like? You don't need special phrasing. Write it the way you'd brief a capable new colleague.

The last question matters most and gets skipped most. "Write an email to parents" leaves everything open. "Write a 120-word email to parents about Friday's early release; warm, plain language, one clear action at the end" tells Claude exactly when it's done.
Several popular cheat sheets boil this down to one line: I want to [task] so that [success criteria]. It's a handy starting shape, not a magic formula.

try.intro: Take a vague request and make it specific, then compare the results.
try.prompt:
Version 1: Write a thank-you note to a coworker.

Version 2: Write a thank-you note to my coworker [name], who [what they did]. It's for a card, so keep it under 60 words. Warm but not gushing, and mention one specific way it helped.
steps: Send Version 2, filled in, in a new chat.
Put the two answers side by side.

check: Version 2 needed fewer edits before I'd actually use it.
I can name which detail made the biggest difference.
I wrote down one success criterion I'll reuse in future prompts.

quiz.q: Which detail most often turns a vague prompt into a useful one?
options: Describing what a good result looks like
quiz.explain: Success criteria, like length, audience, tone, and what must be included, tell Claude what finished means.

quiz.q: What's the best mental model for writing a prompt?
quiz.explain: A new colleague is smart but lacks your context. Give them the goal, the audience, and the finish line.

credit.text: The one-line "I want to [task] so that [success criteria]" shape appears in Ruben Hassid's How to AI infographics.

title: Let Claude ask first
why: You don't have to know everything up front. Letting Claude interview you surfaces the details you didn't think to mention.
idea: When a task has a lot of unknowns, add one sentence to your prompt: "Ask me clarifying questions before you start." Claude will stop and ask about audience, scope, tone, or constraints before writing anything.
This flips the work. Instead of crafting a perfect prompt, you answer a few targeted questions. Depending on where you use Claude, the questions may appear as clickable choices you can tap.
It's most useful for anything with real stakes: a plan, a policy draft, a hard message. For a quick question, skip it.

try.intro: Hand Claude a loose task and let it interview you.
try.prompt: I need to plan [something real you're working on, like a team meeting, a trip, or a class unit]. Ask me clarifying questions until you have enough context, then propose a plan. Ask no more than five questions at a time.
steps: Send the prompt with your real task filled in.
Answer the questions honestly, including "I don't know" where true.

check: At least one question raised something I hadn't thought about.
The plan reflects my answers, not a generic template.
I know when this technique is worth the extra minute and when it isn't.

quiz.q: When is asking Claude to ask clarifying questions most worth it?
options: Tasks with many unknowns or real stakes
quiz.explain: For quick questions it adds friction. For plans, drafts, and decisions, it catches gaps early.

title: Iterate, don't restart
why: The first answer is a draft. The real value comes from the second and third rounds.
idea: When an answer is close but not right, don't start over. Tell Claude specifically what to keep and what to change: "Keep the opening. Cut the third paragraph. Make the ending one sentence." Specific feedback beats "make it better" every time.
Ask for options when you're not sure what you want. "Give me three different openings: one formal, one warm, one blunt" lets you react instead of describing.

Do start fresh when a conversation gets very long or wanders off course. Older details can get less attention as a chat grows. Ask Claude to summarize where things stand, then paste that summary into a new chat.

try.intro: Take one draft through three rounds of specific feedback.
try.prompt: Write a short bio for me to use when I introduce myself at a [meeting, event, or website]. Here's what to include: [3 to 4 facts about you].
steps: Round 1: ask for three versions in different tones.
Round 2: pick one and give one keep, one cut, one change.
Round 3: ask for it at half the length.

check: My final version is noticeably better than the first.
My feedback named specific parts, not just "better" or "shorter."
I know the sign that it's time to start a fresh chat.

quiz.q: Which feedback will get the best revision?
options: "Keep the first line, cut the jargon in paragraph two, end with a question."
quiz.explain: Naming what to keep and what to change gives Claude a clear target.

quiz.q: A chat has gone on for hours and answers are drifting. What helps?
options: Ask for a summary, then continue in a new chat
Switch to a shorter word count
quiz.explain: A fresh chat with a tight summary brings back focus without losing what you decided.

title: Check before you trust
why: Claude is often right, but right often isn't always. A few habits catch most mistakes.
idea: Match your checking to the stakes. A brainstorm needs none. A fact you'll repeat to others, a number in a report, a legal or medical point, or a quote needs a source you've looked at yourself.

Ask Claude to help you check it: "Which of these claims are you least sure about?" and "Give me sources I can verify." With web search on, Claude can cite pages; open them, because a citation is only as good as what the page actually says.

Watch for the classic warning signs: very specific numbers with no source, quotes that sound too perfect, and references to studies, books, or cases you can't find. Those are where hallucinations hide.

try.intro: Run a quick fact-check on Claude's own answer.
try.prompt: Give me five surprising facts about [a topic you're curious about]. For each, rate your confidence as high, medium, or low, and tell me how I could verify it.
steps: Pick the fact with the lowest confidence.
Verify it yourself with a search or a source you trust.

check: I verified at least one claim with a source I looked at myself.
I can name two warning signs of a possible hallucination.
I know which of my own tasks need checking every time.

quiz.q: Claude cites a study you can't find anywhere. What's the most likely explanation?
quiz.explain: Made-up citations are a known failure. If you can't find a source, don't use the claim.

quiz.q: Which task needs the most checking?
options: A statistic you'll present to your board
quiz.explain: Check in proportion to stakes. Numbers you'll repeat publicly need a verified source.
